entry.title: Infrastructure as Code: Make the Change Inspectable

link.title: Infrastructure as Code: Make the Change Inspectable

entry.content:
I completed Infrastructure as Code: The Big Picture by Eugene Meidinger to understand a discipline adjacent to my mobile and backend work. The introductory course gave me a useful frame for a familiar problem: an application depends on configuration that may be harder to inspect than the application code itself.

Using a hypothetical storage-upload feature, I explore how I would review configuration changes and their effect on an application.

The change should have a record

A console setting can be easy to adjust and difficult to explain later. Someone changes a permission or network rule, the immediate issue improves, and the reason disappears into a chat thread.

Infrastructure as Code brings that intended configuration into a versioned artifact. A reviewer can inspect the change, discuss its effects, and connect it to the application’s needs. Versioning preserves the intended configuration and the reasoning behind a change.

A storage upload feature may depend on bucket policy, cross-origin configuration, service identity, and environment variables. Reviewing these alongside the mobile code makes the feature’s assumptions visible.

Declarative describes the result; imperative describes the steps

A declarative approach describes a desired state. An imperative approach specifies operations to perform. Infrastructure automation can use either, and the choice affects how the system handles existing resources and partial failure.

Idempotence means repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once. It is a useful property, but it is not a guarantee that a tool will never replace a resource, lose data, or fail halfway through.

I would also keep provisioning and configuration management distinct when choosing a tool. Creating a cloud resource and configuring software inside a host are related tasks with different responsibilities.

Read the plan as an engineering change

A plan can preview the actions required to align managed resources with configuration. Terraform’s plan documentation describes how it compares configuration and state and proposes changes without applying them.

The review needs to inspect consequences: replacement, deletion, changed access, downtime, and dependency order. “The syntax is valid” is a much narrower statement than “this is safe to apply.”

For an initialized Terraform working directory, an illustrative review sequence is:

terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform plan

Before running these checks, configure the backend, credentials, providers, and target environment. Applying a reviewed plan is a separate step in the deployment procedure.

State deserves its own protection

Terraform uses state to map managed resources to real objects. Its state documentation explains why that mapping is necessary. State needs a storage and access policy appropriate to its contents.

For a collaborative workflow, access control, locking support, backup, and recovery need explicit decisions. HashiCorp’s sensitive data guidance explains that marking a value sensitive can hide it in output while still storing it in state or plan files. Those artifacts should not be committed to a source repository.

I would version the configuration while protecting generated state and plan files according to their contents.

Plan recovery alongside drift detection

Drift is divergence between recorded intent and actual infrastructure. Detecting it gives the team evidence; deciding what to do next requires judgment. An emergency manual change may need to be preserved in code rather than automatically overwritten.

Reverting a commit also does not necessarily restore data or reverse a destructive operation. Recovery may require backups, compatibility work, or a deliberate fix forward. Smaller changes can make the problem easier to reason about, but they do not remove it.

What I want to apply

I would start with one frequently changing, well-understood piece of infrastructure, document its dependencies, and review plans before expanding the scope. The success criterion would be whether another engineer can understand and reproduce the configuration safely.

The course strengthened a principle I already value in application development: a dependable change needs visible intent, clear ownership, and a way to understand failure. Infrastructure makes those requirements especially concrete.
entry.summary: Notes from Eugene Meidinger’s introductory course, with reflections on drift, state, tool choice, and recovery.

entry.title: What a Game Development Course Taught Me About App Design

link.title: What a Game Development Course Taught Me About App Design

entry.content:
I love games, and I am curious about how they are made. That interest led me to complete How to Get Started in Game Development through LA County Library’s instructor-facilitated online learning program on July 19, 2025. The certificate records 24 hours of training.

I approached the introductory course as an app developer looking into another discipline. Games offered a useful perspective on feedback, interaction, production planning, and testing. These are the ideas I took from the course and the questions they raised for my app work.

Feedback is part of the interaction

A game must help the player understand what their action changed. A button press can affect position, resources, progress, or the rules of the next decision. If that relationship is unclear, the player cannot form a reliable mental model.

Apps need the same clarity. Did a task save? Did a payment begin processing? Was a letter scheduled? Animation or color can support that answer, but neither should be the only evidence.

The course made me pay closer attention to the loop between action and feedback. In an app, I would check how clearly the resulting state is visible, understandable, and accessible.

A prototype should answer a question

Interface design and early mockups are useful because they make an idea inspectable before a full implementation exists. The key is deciding what the prototype is meant to teach.

For a game, that might be whether a control scheme feels understandable. For a planning app, it might be whether the distinction between planned and completed work is clear. A focused prototype can answer that interaction question before the backend is complete.

A prototype’s limits should be visible to the people reviewing it. Placeholder state and hardcoded data can make an interaction easier to explore, while leaving persistence, errors, and deployment for later work. Keeping that scope clear makes the feedback more useful.

Choose incentives that fit the product

Games taught me to examine goals, challenges, and rewards more closely. Those mechanisms can help a user learn an interface or notice progress. They can also create unnecessary pressure when copied into the wrong product.

For a productivity app, I would favor clear progress and a neutral presentation of unfinished tasks. For a reflective app, I would make room for a thoughtful session that ends when the person is ready. The incentives should fit the user’s purpose.

That distinction matters to me as both a game enthusiast and someone who studies apps. An enjoyable interaction is valuable, but its success should be defined by the job the product helps someone do.

Production planning exposes dependencies

The course covered the roles and stages involved in making a game, including design, programming, assets, leadership, testing, and publishing. Seeing those responsibilities together was useful for independent app work, where one person may perform several of them.

A feature can depend on artwork, sound, written instructions, permissions, and release preparation as well as code. I would make those dependencies explicit in a small production plan rather than discover them during the final build.

Ownership and asset licensing also need attention. An image downloaded for a prototype may not be appropriate to ship. A practical asset record can preserve where it came from and how it may be used.

Testing includes the experience

A game can launch correctly and still have a confusing objective or an unreachable control. An app can be technically functional and still leave someone unsure what happened.

I would use early interaction reviews alongside technical tests, then check the experience under realistic constraints such as interrupted input, larger text, and poor connectivity where relevant. The aim is to discover where the person’s experience breaks down, even when the underlying feature works.

Course certificate

The course gave me another way to inspect an interaction: what can the person do, what changes, and how do they know? I find that perspective useful well beyond games, and it is one reason I keep learning outside my immediate work.
entry.summary: Reflections on a 24-hour course covering game concepts, interfaces, production, testing, and publishing.

entry.title: Why I Studied Depression as a Software Developer

link.title: Why I Studied Depression as a Software Developer

entry.content:
I enjoy taking classes outside software engineering. Photography changes what I notice in a scene. Design changes how I read an interface. Studying depression made me think more carefully about the person who has to use that interface.

On June 17, 2025, I completed ALLEGRA Learning Solutions’ Certificate in Depression program. My certificate records eight contact hours of continuing education. I took the course to develop a better understanding of people and bring more care to my work as a software engineer.

I chose it because I wanted a better-informed understanding of a subject that affects how people live and work. For me, curiosity about people belongs alongside curiosity about software.

Learn enough to replace assumptions with care

One lesson I took from studying the subject is that familiar words can conceal very different experiences. Depression is not simply a synonym for a difficult day, and an observer cannot infer someone’s condition from a brief interaction.

The National Institute of Mental Health describes depression as a condition that can affect how someone feels, thinks, and handles daily activities. Its overview gives the subject a more accurate foundation than everyday shorthand about mood or motivation.

What I took into my own work was the habit of questioning an assumption before acting on it. A missed task or delayed response tells me very little about the circumstances behind it. Listening is more useful than deciding I already know the explanation.

Ask better questions about attention

Software often asks people to do more: complete another task, respond to another alert, maintain another streak. Those requests may seem small to the person designing them. The person receiving them may already have very little energy or attention available.

I want each interruption to have a purpose and the person to retain control over it.

When designing an app, I would ask whether a reminder can be adjusted, whether an incomplete task is presented neutrally, and whether the user can understand the next step without reading a dense explanation. Those are concrete decisions I can examine as an engineer.

Keep accessibility concrete

Readable text, understandable controls, predictable navigation, and respect for reduced-motion preferences can make an app easier to use. I would verify these qualities directly in the interaction.

I would check the experience with larger text, a screen reader, and an interrupted workflow. I would also inspect error messages for unnecessary blame. “We couldn’t save this. Try again when you’re connected” is more useful than making the user wonder whether their input vanished.

I want to inspect the actual interaction: where it interrupts, what it asks the person to remember, and how clearly it explains a problem.

Two apps, two opportunities for thoughtful design

DoneTodo separates what a person plans to do from what they actually finish. That distinction interests me because a day rarely follows its original plan. The product can acknowledge completed work and present unfinished tasks neutrally.

WayLater lets someone write a message to their future self and open it later. Its value is the space for reflection across time. I would keep that experience private, understandable, and free of pressure to share.

The course sharpened the questions I bring to these design choices: how the product handles attention, preserves control, and makes the next step manageable.

The certificate and the continuing lesson

I will remember the course when a product decision seems obvious from behind my own screen. It gives me a reason to slow down, consider another person’s circumstances, and check whether the next step is as clear and manageable as I think it is.
entry.summary: A personal reflection on an eight-hour education program and the questions it raised about attention, empathy, and product design.

entry.title: A Lean Testing Strategy for Independent iOS Apps

link.title: A Lean Testing Strategy for Independent iOS Apps

entry.content:
Developing my own Swift apps drew me toward quality engineering. I enjoyed building the interaction, but I was especially interested in the defect that appeared only after an unusual sequence of actions. Writing test plans and learning automation gave me a way to pursue those questions more systematically.

For an independent app, I would organize testing around quick feedback on logic, focused UI coverage where interaction matters, and clear evidence about the release candidate. These examples show how that strategy fits the kinds of apps I build.

Move rules where they can be exercised directly

A view can display state and translate gestures into actions. The calculation, validation, or state-transition rules should be testable without tapping through the entire interface.

A calculator provides a compact example. Operator precedence, repeated equals, backspace, percent, and entry after a completed calculation are behavior questions. The rules should be explicit before the tests become authoritative.

// Illustrative test for an application-defined calculator model.
func testMultiplicationPrecedesAddition() {
    var calculator = Calculator()
    calculator.enter(["2", "+", "3", "×", "4", "="])
    XCTAssertEqual(calculator.display, "14")
}

Choosing Decimal supports decimal arithmetic. The model also needs explicit rounding, precision, and domain rules, with tests for the expected behavior.

Use UI tests for questions the model cannot answer

UI tests can check whether a control is reachable, whether a sheet blocks navigation, and whether a result remains readable with larger text. They complement the rules exercised by model tests.

Appium with Python and pytest is one possible route. The following illustrative session uses the options-based API described in the Appium Python client documentation:

from appium import webdriver
from appium.options.ios import XCUITestOptions

options = XCUITestOptions().load_capabilities({
    "platformName": "iOS",
    "appium:automationName": "XCUITest",
    "appium:udid": simulator_udid,
    "appium:app": simulator_app_path,
})
driver = webdriver.Remote("http://127.0.0.1:4723", options=options)
try:
    verify_critical_flow(driver)
finally:
    driver.quit()

Here, simulator_udid, simulator_app_path, and verify_critical_flow stand for the project’s own configuration and assertions. The Appium server, XCUITest driver, simulator runtime, and simulator-compatible build must be set up separately. Session reuse can reduce startup work, but every test still needs a controlled starting state.

Give automation and accessibility separate attention

A stable accessibility identifier helps a UI test find an element. A meaningful accessibility label and value help someone using VoiceOver understand it. They serve distinct purposes and need separate review.

Text(display)
    .accessibilityIdentifier("calculator.result")
    .accessibilityLabel("Result")
    .accessibilityValue(display)

Apple documents identifiers and labels separately. I would verify the spoken experience as well as the locator. Localization, focus order, contrast, and larger text introduce questions a stable ID does not answer.

Build a small, trustworthy release check

A useful candidate check might include installation and launch, the primary flow, persisted state after relaunch, and one meaningful failure path. Device testing remains important for behavior simulators do not represent completely.

Test output should identify the build, environment, action sequence, and observed result. Screenshots and logs help only when they correspond to the actual failure and avoid sensitive data.

I would investigate flakes as defects in the test system: timing assumptions, shared state, unstable locators, or environment problems. Blind retries can make a pipeline green without making its evidence stronger.

Grow coverage from risk

A newly found bug is an opportunity to add the smallest test that reproduces it. A feature with several states may need a transition table before automation. A simple visual change may need a device review rather than a large new suite.

The maintenance question is practical: when a test fails, does it tell me something useful about the app? Coverage should grow from those answers, from reported defects, and from features whose failure would matter most to the person using them.
entry.summary: A practical approach to logic tests, UI automation, accessibility, and release checks for independent iOS apps.

entry.title: What Functional, Integration, Smoke, and Regression Tests Actually Tell Us

link.title: What Functional, Integration, Smoke, and Regression Tests Actually Tell Us

entry.content:
When I began writing more deliberate test plans for my apps, I found that test names were less useful than test questions. “We have integration tests” says little without knowing which boundary they exercise. “The regression suite passed” says little without knowing which behaviors it revisits.

These names describe different aspects of testing. Functional describes the behavior being checked; integration describes an interaction boundary; smoke describes a limited readiness check; regression describes testing after change. They can overlap. I find the names most useful when they explain what a test checks and what its failure tells us. The ISTQB Foundation Level syllabus distinguishes test levels, test types, and testing after change.

Functional: does the behavior match the requirement?

A functional test checks an expected capability at a unit, API, component, or end-to-end level. Its dependencies and interface follow from the behavior being checked.

Consider a cart requirement: adding two items should produce the correct total. An isolated model test can check calculation quickly. An API test can check the returned total. A UI test can check what the user sees. Those tests ask related questions at different boundaries.

This illustrative XCTest example focuses on behavior without a network dependency:

func testAddingTwoItemsUpdatesTotal() {
    var cart = Cart()
    cart.add(price: Decimal(string: "3.50")!, quantity: 2)
    XCTAssertEqual(cart.total, Decimal(7))
}

This focused example checks quantity multiplication. Tax, rounding policy, and currency rules would each need additional cases.

Integration: do the components agree?

An integration test exercises interaction across a meaningful boundary: service and database, client and API, or publisher and consumer. The setup should state which components are real and which surrounding dependencies are substituted.

A contract test can verify an agreed request and response shape without exercising the entire deployed system. Pact’s documentation explains how consumer tests and provider verification check different sides of that agreement. The deployed connection may still fail because of permissions, configuration, or runtime behavior outside the contract.

For a mobile API, I would inspect field names, optional values, serialization, authorization errors, and pagination. A fake that always returns the same ideal object can hide the very mismatch an integration test is meant to find.

Test data also needs isolation. A convenient shared environment can introduce changing state and unclear ownership. Disposable databases or uniquely scoped fixtures are useful where the system supports them.

Smoke: is the candidate usable enough to continue?

A smoke suite is a deliberately small set of high-value checks. It may include launch, sign-in, and one critical transaction. It can exercise business logic; its defining feature is narrow scope and fast evidence about basic viability.

The suite should remain small enough to run at an important decision point, such as after deployment. Including the principal user workflow gives more useful readiness evidence than a health endpoint alone.

Failure should have a defined response. That may block promotion or trigger investigation. The team should define when failure blocks promotion, triggers investigation, or warrants rollback.

Regression: did a change break behavior we rely on?

Regression testing revisits existing behavior after change. Tests for historical defects are particularly useful examples, but the category is broader than bug history.

When fixing a defect, I first want to reproduce the original failure and confirm that the fix resolves it. That is confirmation testing. Regression testing asks the wider question: what else might the change have affected? A test for the original defect can remain in future regression coverage, with a linked issue explaining why it exists.

Put cost and evidence together

Question Useful evidence Common blind spot
Does the rule work? Focused functional assertion Unrealistic fixture
Do components agree? Boundary exercised with stated dependencies Environment drift
Is this build viable? Short critical-path smoke flow Suite expands until rarely run
Did behavior change unexpectedly? Repeatable regression coverage Missing original conditions

Runtime, reliability, and diagnostic value belong in the same discussion. A quick assertion on an unrealistic fixture can miss the problem. A slower boundary test may be worth keeping if it catches a costly failure and tells us where to investigate. I would measure those properties before setting a suite budget.

The part I enjoy is turning an uncertain behavior into a precise question. A good suite makes those questions repeatable and makes the next failure easier to investigate.
entry.summary: Choosing tests by the behavior, boundary, and release risk they help investigate.

entry.title: From Shipping Apps to Asking Better Quality Questions

link.title: From Shipping Apps to Asking Better Quality Questions

entry.content:
Building the consumer and technician apps at SupTech gave me a broad view of software delivery. I worked on the Flutter clients, API integration, interface decisions, and the sequence that connected orders, location, chat, and payment. I also helped clarify requirements and coordinate work around them.

The experience showed me that I enjoy more than adding features. I like finding the point where a system’s assumptions stop holding: a state that cannot be reached cleanly, a request that can be repeated unsafely, or a screen that tells the user something the backend has not confirmed.

In February 2025, I was deciding where to take that interest next. Building two products had given me breadth. I wanted an environment where I could turn that experience into deeper engineering judgment.

What building from zero required

The two apps represented different roles in one service workflow. Consumers requested help and followed an order. Technicians discovered work, accepted it, communicated, and reported progress.

Implementing those clients required attention to both shared infrastructure and role-specific behavior. Authentication, localization, and API models offered opportunities for reuse. The decisions each person needed to make were different.

The integrations also pushed me beyond the widget layer: Stripe payment and connected accounts, location updates and matching, push notifications, chat persistence, and an AI-assisted repair flow. Working with Node.js/Firebase and a Java/MySQL backend made the client/server boundary especially important.

The work required decisions across those tools: who owns an order transition, which response is authoritative, and what the person sees while the system is uncertain.

Product understanding made the technical work stronger

Requirements changed as the business refined its workflow. I helped turn requests into concrete behaviors, record scope, and show internal builds for feedback.

That work improved my ability to explain dependencies. A different dispatch rule can affect stored profiles, eligibility, notifications, and the map. A payment change can affect cancellation and support. The UI is often where a requirement becomes visible, but the impact extends farther.

I also learned that a clear explanation of a tradeoff is part of ownership. If a new priority changes the release plan, the decision should be visible rather than absorbed silently by the developer.

The bugs were often the most interesting part

I enjoyed tracing unexpected behavior through the full flow. A reported failure gives me a concrete investigation: what happened, under which conditions, and how the same defect could be prevented from returning.

That interest led me toward more deliberate test planning and learning automation. I wanted to make the important questions repeatable: can two users accept the same order, does an interrupted request leave a recoverable state, and does the UI distinguish a failure from an empty result?

Testing is especially appealing to me because it combines technical reasoning with product context. A useful assertion connects directly to behavior the product promises.

What I wanted from the next environment

I wanted to keep building while developing more depth in quality, automation, and collaborative engineering. A team with thoughtful review and opportunities to learn from other engineers would help turn broad startup experience into more precise judgment.

I wanted to learn how engineers work on larger systems: how components interact, how releases are validated, and how a team decides that the evidence is sufficient. Working alongside people with different areas of expertise was as appealing as the technical complexity.

My independent app work also remained important. Designing and shipping my own products keeps me close to the user experience and gives me a place to explore ideas directly.

The direction I took from this work

SupTech strengthened my ability to carry a product through ambiguity and connect implementation to a working release. It also clarified the problems that hold my attention: an unreliable transition, a missing assumption, or an interaction that looks simple until someone uses it differently.

I value that combination of building and investigating. It lets me approach quality as part of the engineering work from the beginning, with attention to both the system’s behavior and the person relying on it.

You can reach me at tongzemao@gmail.com.
entry.summary: A reflection on building two service apps at SupTech and the engineering direction that experience clarified.

entry.title: Real-Time Chat Starts With Durable Messages

link.title: Real-Time Chat Starts With Durable Messages

entry.content:
In a service app, a message can change what happens next. A customer sends a photo before the technician arrives. A technician asks about access or explains a delay. If that information disappears or arrives twice, the conversation becomes another problem the two people have to solve.

I worked on Flutter chat flows tied to orders. The interface needed to feel immediate, while the underlying system needed to preserve a coherent conversation. Those goals require different pieces of state.

Authorize access to each conversation

An order-scoped conversation gives messages a clear purpose. The backend still needs to verify that the current user is allowed to read or write that conversation. The server must check membership for the requested conversation. Firebase’s security rules guide illustrates the separate work of checking authentication and access to particular data.

The message model should include a stable ID, conversation ID, sender, content type, and server-assigned ordering information. Media references and system events need explicit types rather than overloaded text fields.

A client should not be able to claim another sender ID or author a trusted system event. “Service has started” should derive from a verified order transition, not simply appear because a device submitted that sentence.

Keep local display and persistence distinct

Optimistic UI can show a message immediately. That local message should carry a sending state until the server acknowledges it. If transmission fails, the user needs a clear retry action rather than a bubble that appears delivered. Flutter’s optimistic state guide makes the same distinction between immediate feedback and the result of the underlying operation.

This illustrative model makes the distinction visible:

enum DeliveryState { sending, sent, failed }

class PendingMessage {
  const PendingMessage({
    required this.clientId,
    required this.text,
    required this.deliveryState,
  });
  final String clientId;
  final String text;
  final DeliveryState deliveryState;
}

A stable client-generated ID can help reconcile the optimistic item with the persisted one. Reusing that ID during a retry gives the backend a way to recognize the same logical message. Preventing duplicate storage still requires the server to enforce uniqueness within an appropriate conversation and sender scope.

“Sent,” “delivered,” and “read” should identify separate milestones: server persistence, receipt by another device, and the recipient’s read acknowledgement.

Reconcile messages after reconnecting

A stream, WebSocket, or polling endpoint can supply updates. After reconnecting, the client may receive items it already has or discover a gap. Merging by ID and fetching after a known cursor is safer than appending every event to a list. Firestore documents snapshot listeners and query cursors as separate tools; the application still has to define its own reconciliation behavior.

Server timestamps are useful, but ordering may need a tie-breaker or sequence. A device clock should not decide the authoritative order of a multi-device conversation.

Pagination matters for history. Loading a bounded recent page keeps startup manageable; older messages can load when requested. The merge should preserve scroll position rather than jump the reader away from the message they are inspecting.

Media has its own lifecycle

Selecting a photo, uploading it, and sending the message are separate steps. The UI should show upload progress or failure and avoid claiming a media message is sent before the attachment is available.

The server needs content validation, access controls, and a retention policy. A public URL that anyone can open may not be appropriate for private service details. Cancelling or abandoning an upload also raises a cleanup question.

Notifications bring the person back

Push notifications help when the conversation is not open. They should point to the persisted conversation, which the client loads after checking the session and access.

An old notification might refer to a completed order or a conversation the user can no longer access. The destination needs to handle that honestly. Notification previews should also consider what private content becomes visible on a lock screen.

Test the conversation as a sequence

I would test sending while offline, retrying after an ambiguous timeout, reconnecting after several messages, duplicate events, pagination, media failure, and leaving the screen during an async response. Multi-device read state adds another useful set of cases.

My review would follow the states that matter to the person using the chat: whether a retry creates a duplicate, whether a photo has uploaded, and where an old notification leads. The interface should make each of those states understandable.
entry.summary: Designing order-scoped chat around authorization, optimistic state, synchronization, media, and notifications.

entry.title: Location-Based Job Discovery With Google Maps

link.title: Location-Based Job Discovery With Google Maps

entry.content:
I used Google Maps in Flutter service apps to show nearby work and connect map selections with job details. Behind that screen, the backend updated nearby-order data as technician locations changed. The pins were the visible result of several decisions about permissions, matching, and freshness.

Reviewing the feature, I pay particular attention to what a coordinate means at the moment the user sees it. A map can look convincing even when the position is stale or the job is no longer available.

Distinguish a position from a reliable position

Latitude and longitude need context: when were they observed, how accurate are they, and what permission did the user grant? A recent approximate location and an old precise location carry different uncertainties.

I would include freshness and accuracy in matching decisions and explain when an update is unavailable. If a demo uses a default city, label it clearly as a fallback rather than the user’s position.

A pinned service address is a different concept from the device’s location. The customer may request service somewhere else. Those fields should have separate names and ownership.

Permission denial is an ordinary state

The app needs to handle unavailable services, denied permission, permanently denied permission, and approximate access. The useful fallback depends on the feature. A user might browse by a manually selected area even if device location is unavailable.

Only enable the map’s location display after access has been granted. Google’s Flutter location example describes the permission prerequisite. Background tracking requires separate platform configuration; Android’s location-permission guide distinguishes foreground, background, precise, and approximate access.

I would request the access needed for the current action and explain its purpose. Asking for every possible location capability on first launch makes that explanation harder to understand.

Separate discovery from assignment

The nearby-job feed used coordinates to select relevant orders. A distance threshold can be a useful eligibility rule, but the displayed feed may become stale between loading and acceptance.

The server must recheck availability when the technician accepts. The map should then handle a conflict by refreshing the order and explaining the new state.

A radius match describes geographic eligibility. Road distance and travel time require a routing service and additional assumptions, with arrival estimates presented separately from the radius filter.

Keep the map and the list in agreement

Stable order IDs make markers easier to update and help link map selections to list rows. A selected pin should refer to the same order the detail screen loads.

Loading a new position after the map is created may require an explicit camera update; an initial camera setting is not an ongoing location subscription. The app should also respect the user’s exploration instead of recentering the map every time a new coordinate arrives.

For dense results, I would consider clustering or a smaller query area to keep the map usable as the data grows.

Treat location updates as a cost and privacy decision

More frequent updates can improve freshness while consuming battery, network traffic, and backend work. The appropriate policy depends on whether a technician is browsing, traveling for an active order, or off duty.

A useful extension would stop unnecessary sharing and use movement, time, and workflow state to decide when another update is worth sending. Access and retention rules should also limit who can inspect a person’s location history.

Validate behavior beyond the simulator

I would check permission denial, approximate access, a stale backend location, poor connectivity, an order disappearing during refresh, and switching between map and list. Different screen sizes and text lengths also affect marker and detail presentation.

A useful map keeps the visible pins, the job list, and the server’s current order state in agreement. That is the behavior I would verify before adding more visual detail or more frequent location updates.
entry.summary: Lessons from location-based service apps: permissions, stale coordinates, matching, and map state.

entry.title: Building a Reliable Mobile Payment Flow With Stripe

link.title: Building a Reliable Mobile Payment Flow With Stripe

entry.content:
In my Flutter service apps, a customer could pay for a job and a technician could receive a transfer after the work. The payment sheet was one part of that flow. The backend also had to keep the payment, order, and recipient account in agreement when requests were delayed or interrupted.

I implemented PaymentIntents, customer credentials, connected-account transfers, and backend scheduling with Firebase Functions and Firestore. For an extension of this integration, I would focus on recovery across payment, order, and transfer states.

The server decides what is being paid

The client can identify an order and request checkout. The server should authenticate the user, verify ownership, determine the payable amount from trusted records, and select the currency. Accepting an arbitrary client-supplied amount would let a modified app redefine the transaction.

A PaymentIntent tracks a payment lifecycle. Stripe recommends creating one for each order or customer session and reusing it where appropriate; its integration guide explains that relationship.

Here is an illustrative server operation, after validation and order lookup:

const intent = await stripe.paymentIntents.create(
  {
    amount: order.amountMinorUnits,
    currency: order.currency,
    customer: customer.stripeId,
    metadata: { orderId: order.id },
  },
  { idempotencyKey: `order:${order.id}:payment:${order.paymentVersion}` }
);

Persist the relationship between the order and PaymentIntent, and handle price or order revisions deliberately. Reusing that relationship keeps repeated checkout attempts traceable.

Separate SDK access from authority

The mobile app receives the limited information required to present the payment interface. In customer-based integrations, a short-lived customer credential can grant SDK access to customer resources. The backend retains authority over the amount, order relationship, and financial updates.

Stripe’s secret API key stays on the server. Payment client secrets and customer credentials should also be handled as sensitive values, with access scoped to the authenticated transaction and no routine logging.

The exact mobile SDK configuration depends on the integration and version; follow the supported SDK path for the deployed client.

Reconcile payment state on the server

A client callback is useful for the immediate interface, but server-side reconciliation determines the authoritative order payment state. The user may close the app, lose connectivity, or complete a payment that requires asynchronous processing.

Stripe’s webhook guidance covers signature verification, duplicate events, and delivery behavior. I would verify the signature against the raw request body before accepting the event, store a durable receipt, and make subsequent business updates idempotent.

Handle events that arrive out of order. If an update is ambiguous or stale, retrieve the current payment state before deciding the next business transition.

Connect introduces another lifecycle

A technician connected account can have incomplete onboarding or unavailable capabilities. Check the account’s current status and required capabilities after the onboarding return.

A transfer moves funds from the platform to the connected Stripe account. A payout moves available funds to an external account such as a bank account. The distinction matters for status text, support investigation, and scheduling. Stripe documents those boundaries; delaying funds should not be described as Stripe escrow.

A delayed transfer job needs ownership, retry rules, a stable idempotency key, and reconciliation when the process stops after the API succeeds. A refund may require a separate transfer reversal decision, depending on the charge model. Record and reconcile each fund movement explicitly.

Test the uncertain moments

Beyond a successful card payment, I would check a declined method, authentication interruption, duplicate checkout requests, a delayed webhook, an incomplete connected account, insufficient available balance, and a partial refund.

The UI should explain whether payment is processing, failed, or confirmed, and check the existing attempt before inviting the user to pay again.

The cases I find most revealing are the uncertain ones: the server succeeded but the client timed out, a webhook arrived twice, or a transfer stopped midway through reconciliation. Testing those transitions is how I would establish confidence in the order history.
entry.summary: What integrating Stripe taught me about server-owned amounts, asynchronous payment state, Connect, and recovery.

entry.title: A Flutter Network Layer With Dio

link.title: A Flutter Network Layer With Dio

entry.content:
My Flutter apps shared a custom Dio wrapper for configuration, headers, interceptors, and uploads. It reduced repeated setup, but reviewing it also showed where one global policy could accidentally override the needs of an individual request.

The boundary I now aim for is a small configured client, with explicit policies for authentication, response parsing, and retries. A feature should still be able to tell whether it is performing a read, uploading a file, or creating something that must not be repeated.

Share configuration without requiring global state

A shared Dio configuration gives the app consistent timeouts, authentication handling, and environment selection. Dio’s documentation describes instance options, interceptors, cancellation, and multipart requests.

A singleton is one way to distribute that configuration. Passing the configured client into repositories is another, and it makes tests easier to isolate. I care more about consistent ownership than the particular pattern.

This illustrative setup shows a configured client passed into a feature API:

Dio createApiClient(String baseUrl) => Dio(BaseOptions(
  baseUrl: baseUrl,
  connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 15),
  receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
  sendTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
));

class OrderApi {
  OrderApi(this.client);
  final Dio client;
}

The example timeout values should be adapted to the operation. Uploads and ordinary reads may warrant different policies. Environment selection should also be intentional; changing a global base URL while requests are in flight can make failures hard to reproduce.

Let interceptors handle cross-cutting concerns

Authentication headers, safe request diagnostics, and standard transport error mapping fit naturally into interceptors. Credentials should only be attached to the intended API origin, including when a client follows redirects or is reused for another host. Business decisions generally belong closer to the feature.

For example, a response envelope may contain an application code, but that convention should be parsed only for endpoints that use it. A successful file download or a 204 No Content response should not fail because it lacks data['code'] == 200.

The wrapper should preserve useful evidence: HTTP status, application error code, operation, and an appropriate correlation ID. Turning every failure into a string discards information the UI and tests may need.

Define retry policy for each operation

A read that fails before receiving a response can often be retried. A request to create an order or transfer money is different. The server may have applied it even if the client timed out.

For those operations, I would use server-supported idempotency and a way to query the resulting state. Repeating the HTTP call without that agreement risks repeating the action.

Authentication refresh has its own concurrency concern. Several requests can fail authorization together, and independent refresh attempts can race. A coordinated in-flight refresh is a useful pattern, with a strict retry limit and an escape from the interceptor loop.

Treat uploads as a distinct operation

Multipart uploads need the correct content type and boundary. Dio can build them from FormData; forcing a URL-encoded content type over that request is the wrong default.

// Illustrative upload; server-side validation is still required.
final form = FormData.fromMap({
  'file': await MultipartFile.fromFile(file.path, filename: fileName),
});
await client.post('/uploads', data: form, cancelToken: cancelToken);

Progress, cancellation, size limits, and validation are also part of the experience. For a retry, create fresh FormData and MultipartFile objects; Dio documents this requirement because an earlier request can finalize their streams.

Log what helps, omit what harms

The method, route pattern, status, and duration are often sufficient to begin investigation. Tokens, passwords, raw payment data, and full private response bodies are poor logging defaults. Debug mode alone does not make realistic user data safe to print.

The UI should receive a meaningful error category, such as offline, timeout, unauthorized, validation failure, or conflict. Raw exception text rarely gives the user a useful next step.

Test the policy at the boundary

I would verify header injection, cancellation, known response shapes, empty success responses, malformed data, concurrent refresh, and retry behavior. A fake transport can cover these cases without contacting a live backend.

I would keep the wrapper small enough that its behavior can be read and tested. Its value is consistent defaults, useful failure evidence, and a deliberate escape for requests that need a different policy.
entry.summary: Refining a Flutter Dio wrapper around authentication, error semantics, uploads, retries, and testability.
